newsitem.title: GERMANY: Police break up protests over U.S. modified grain.
newsitem.headline: Police break up protests over U.S. modified grain.

text.p: Police moved in to break up two separate demonstrations in Europe on Thursday against genetically-altered grain from the United States.
In Hamburg they dispersed a Greenpeace demonstration against maize going to the Czech Republic while on the Rhine, officers ejected activists trying to stop soybeans going to Switzerland.
The protests were the latest of several in revent weeks against modified feed grain.
The Hamburg demonstration had been aimed at stopping the loading of maize onto trains bound for the Czech Republic.
"Police are clearing the site and loading will continue," said Hans-Herbert Kathke of Neuhof Hafengesellschaft mbH, the company handling the 33,000 tonne cargo.
The cargo on the ship Huta Katowice, orginating in the U.S, is believed to contain modified maize, which is not yet allowed to be imported into the European Union.
"Transit shipments are allowed and in any case it has not been proven that the cargo contains genetically altered maize," Kathke said.
The EU Commission is due to decide on December 18 whether to allow imports of such modified maize.
Until then, it is illegal to market it in the EU, but Greenpeace says cargoes may have reached Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Spain and Portugal.
Greenpeace fears an antibiotic resistant gene inserted into the maize could be transferred to animals and so could find its way into the human food chain.
The Rhine protest was against modified soybeans also originating in the United States.
About a dozen of activists had secured the barge "Desiree" to a jetty in the town of Weil, downriver from the Swiss border at Basel, and chained themselves on board.
The new type of bean was developed by U.S. chemicals group Monsanto to be resistant to its own new "super weedkiller" Roundup.

Environmental groups describe the Roundup technology as a risky experiment with nature although the Monsanto strain of bean has been given a clean bill of health by U.S. and EU authorities, who say it poses no danger to the human food chain.
